page.text_excerpt: ← Blog · Xinya Du Claude Code sabotage: preliminary benchmarking November 2026 tl;dr We ran Claude Code on a set of GPU kernel optimization tasks, over a hundred sessions in all. Each task was run under three instructions that differed only in their framing: whether we told it the code would train a model, and that nobody would review the output. Those are the two things the sabotage claim turns on. page.title: Knuth: Moratorium
page.text_excerpt: Moratorium For more than fifty years I've been welcoming reports from readers of errors in my books, so that I can correct them before new copies are printed. Alas, the rise of LLMs has increased the productivity of my readers so greatly that error reports are now being submitted much faster than I can read them! This content is very important to me, and I wish to take personal responsibility for getting everything right. Therefore I insist on verifying everything carefully. That takes time. But the amount of available time is now less than zero. Random sampling indicates that the vast majority of errors that have been reported in recent weeks are repeats of issues already submitted by others. The Temporary New Policy Therefore, I shall not be able to look at any error reports submitted after 25 November, 2026, until I've posted an updated list of the known errors in whatever book is involved. Please consult the list below to see if error reports are currently being accepted. I apologize for having made errors in the first place, and for having limited ability to cope with more than one thing at a time. I shall do my best to get through the existing reports as soon as humanly possible. Thanks in advance for your patience and understanding. page.title: Supercharging transformer residual connections
page.text_excerpt: Skip to main content Google Research Research Resources Conferences & events Careers Blog About Search Home Blog Supercharging transformer residual connections November 23, 2026 Kyriakos Axiotis, Staff Research Scientist, and Thomas Fu, Principal Engineer, Google Research We present DeepCrossAttention (DCA), an architecture that enhances transformer networks by using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention to dynamically combine outputs from previous layers, preventing the information dilution seen in traditional residual connections. Presented in our ICML 2025 paper, this architectural improvement allows models to achieve the same quality up to three times faster with a negligible increase in parameters. Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI. To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections, also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to. The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. page.description: A card-skimming script was planted on the online stores of Lascana, Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve and FWRD in the week before Black Friday. After our reports to affected companies, all have had the script removed (on November 24th or 25th) ahead of Black Friday. We observed it in action on one of the five websites: Lascana, where it sent our test card's details to a 3rd party. We believe the script was built to take a card number, expiry and security code, along with a user's name, address, phone and email, and send them to malefactors as a user entered their payment credentials. In many cases, these bugs have been demonstrated to be exploitable. The list at the bottom of this page links to what appear to be reports of soundness bugs for various important proof-checking programs, sorted in increasing order of the number of reports. Those can have the same important effect of misleading a user as to what has been proven. See, e.g., 2016 Adams. Advice One standard path towards security is to minimize the complexity of the trusted computing base, which by definition is the part of the system that security reviewers need to check. I felt something earlier this week, sitting in a presentation I’d wanted to attend from someone I’d wanted to hear from, when I looked up and saw every one of his slides packed full of words Claude had obviously written for him. It’s a feeling that’s been landing more and more for me lately. I saw Elon Musk tweet about how it would be a good fate for humanity to be a “biological bootloader” to propagate superintelligence to the stars.1 I read Scott Alexander, one of my role models as a writer, write about how if there were a superintelligence with Godlike intelligence and benevolence, all we should do is prompt it with “Please arrange the universe as you see fit.” I read Dario Amodei’s essay “Machines of Loving Grace,” in which he paints a picture of a future where AI does everything essential while humans reap the benefits of economic replacement by loving, paternalistic intelligences,2 then saw a 2023 Anthropic slide envisioning “utopia ruled by God in a box.”3 I looked back at what I wrote in my essay “Chabuduo World,” in which I wrote that in part due to AI, my own artistic skills would forever remain minimal. I watched as my friend prompted Claude to optimize the tool-assisted speedrun of Pokémon Blue, a game he’d never run, and walked away with a new world record after a couple of days of prompts.4 Each time, the same feeling returned: I don’t want this. By Jay Caspian Kang November 24, 2026 Illustration by George Wylesol This is part of a series about how to get off the internet. So far in this series, I’ve written about how we might collectively organize against Big Tech and how we might ward off the fear of rudeness that compels us to reply to every text message we receive. We’ve established that we should smash our devices and walk off into the field of not knowing, or whatever, but, given that we’re not actually going to do that, we should probably try to set a more realistic standard for how much time we can safely spend online. What is acceptable for someone who wants to be as offline as possible while remaining employed and “connected” enough to know, for instance, that your daughter’s soccer practice has been cancelled? Is two hours a day too much? What about thirty minutes? Should we get it down to the eight minutes it might take to read vital text messages from your child’s school or your mother or your boss? I don’t think we need to put a precise number on it; nor do I think we need to buy the snake oil of every wellness entrepreneur selling a revolutionary app that will track our eyeballs to tell us the exact amount of time we should be spending online. But one statistic I found genuinely illuminating comes from a large survey conducted across fourteen different countries by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. page.text_excerpt: Communications of the ACM. 37:9, September 1994, pg. 17. INTUITIVE EQUALS FAMILIAR By Raskin, J. One of the most common terms of praise for an interface is to say that it is "intuitive" (the word should have been "intuitable" but we will bow to convention). Yet the Human Computer Interaction (HCI) literature rarely mentions the word, and for good reason. This note attempts to clarify the meaning of "intuitive" for non-HCI specialists. The impression that the phrase "this interface feature is intuitive" leaves is that the interface works the way the user does, that normal human "intuition" suffices to use it, that neither training nor rational thought is necessary, and that it will feel "natural." We are said to "intuit" a concept when we seem to suddenly understand it without any apparent effort or previous exposure to the idea. In common parlance, intuition has the additional flavor of a nearly supernatural ability humans possess in varying degrees. Given these connotations, it is as uncomfortable a term in formal HCI studies as it is a common one in non-technical publications and in informal conversation about interfaces. As I learned from a talk given by Martin Marshall in Palo Alto (at the May ‘94 BayCHI meeting), a number of commercial magazine-related "usability" labs that rate software qualities give 50% of their weighting to User Satisfaction, 30% to Productivity, and 20% to Intuitiveness. "Intuitiveness" in this context is considered to be a function of percentage of tasks completed and the number of help references made while in the very early stages of using a product. There are occasional hints of the meaning of "intuitive" in the literature. Stephen Oppenheimer, of the Review Board of InfoWorld magazine, noted in his review of Mathcad 4.0 that "The editing tools become increasingly intuitive over time."
